# Ultimate Ramp Marketing Archive

> An independent, opinionated study of Ramp marketing for founders and marketers.

All public pages contain their complete text, reported metrics and original source links in HTML. JavaScript is only needed for enhanced interactions. Open native disclosure sections to inspect post-level metrics. Company and partner claims retain their attribution; Notes explain limitations.

## Indexes
- [Campaign index JSON](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/archive.json)
- [Sitemap](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/sitemap.xml)

## Case studies
- [Incentives: reward the behavior](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/campaign/incentives/): A prize can buy a click. The rules decide what happens next. Ramp’s offers are more useful to study side by side: some pay for a conversation, others for product use, approval or repeated attendance.
- [Introducing Glass](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/campaign/glass/): “We needed this ourselves” is easy to say. Ramp launched Glass with details of its own use: employees editing shared knowledge, capturing customer requests and sending updates. Those examples made the origin story inspectable before the early-access invitation.
- [Sports partnerships: beyond the logo](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/campaign/sports-partnerships/): A sports logo earns recognition. The finance work behind a team can earn a business buyer’s interest. Ramp’s partnerships combine those jobs in different ways, and the distinction is worth keeping visible.
- [Tony Stock: Pro Trader](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/campaign/tony-stock/): What if we took a simple (slightly silly) idea and turned it into a whole world? Take a man famous for loving ramps and put him in a Ramp ad. Tony Hawk has to give up skating and start trading stocks under witness protection - giving birth to "Tony Stock".
- [Product launches: make the work visible](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/campaign/product-launches/): Ramp repeatedly starts with a task finance teams recognize: review a purchase, process an invoice, close the books, get paid. Comparing the launches shows how a broad automation promise becomes a specific job a buyer can judge.
- [Partnerships: build a route to the buyer](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/campaign/partner-distribution/): A partnership earns its place when it changes how a buyer hears about, pays for or benefits from a product. These three relationships solve different parts of that journey.
- [Country launches: the UK and Canada](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/campaign/uk/): A country launch has two jobs: prove the product understands the local work, and get the news beyond the company account. Ramp used UK-specific finance details and a customer story for the first. A coordinated employee posting wave helped with the second.
- [Bill Pay: The Musical](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/campaign/bill-pay-musical/): Paying bills is spectacularly untheatrical. Ramp made that mismatch the joke and backed it with a real Broadway production. They wrote original songs, choreography, and hired a professional cast which made the show much more than a marketing gimmick.
- [Router.com](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/campaign/router/): Developers choose models repeatedly, and every choice affects cost. Router put Ramp’s spending promise at that decision point. A useful tool gave the brand a way into a technical audience’s daily work.
- [$500,000 Treasury Sweepstakes](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/campaign/treasury-sweepstakes/): A $500,000 prize is difficult to ignore. The more interesting work happened in the entry rules: open an account, hold a balance, pay a bill. The promotion introduced prospects to the actions Ramp wanted them to repeat as customers.
- [The Kumar Method](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/campaign/kumar-method/): Kumar appeared out of nowhere: a swaggering accountant whose videos went viral and left everyone asking for his method. Then he disappeared. Was he a Ramp plant all along? Nobody knows. By the time Ramp appeared, the audience already had a mystery to solve: where had Kumar gone, and would he ever release his method? A book on Ramp’s site finally gave that running joke somewhere to go.
- [Ramp Stack](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/campaign/ramp-stack/): An accountant can judge finished work. Ramp introduced Stack with a more demanding question than “does this AI sound clever?”: can it complete accounting tasks? The benchmark gave buyers something closer to their own standard of proof.
- [On the Company Card](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/campaign/company-card-series/): A corporate card looks the same in every product shot. The businesses using it do not. “On the Company Card” made a customer’s working life the subject, giving Ramp a repeatable format with more to watch than a testimonial.
- [Marketing to AI agents](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/campaign/marketing-ai-agents/): If an assistant is researching software for a buyer, can an offer survive the summary? Ramp tested that smaller, answerable question. It put an incentive where AI agents could read it and checked whether their answers passed it along.
- [Brian Bowl](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/campaign/brian-bowl/): After Brian’s Office, the audience already knew what one Brian looked like at work. Ramp cloned him for its Super Bowl ad to make a different point: automation lets one team do the work of many.
- [Funeral for the Penny](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/campaign/penny-funeral/): If America was going to stop making pennies, Ramp thought the penny deserved a proper send-off. The funeral took an abstract change in how money works and gave people a ritual they already knew how to join.
- [LinkedIn account-based advertising waves](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/campaign/linkedin-abm/): “We can save your company money” asks the reader to do the translation. Ramp’s account-specific LinkedIn ads did some of it for them. A named company, a recognizable spending problem and a relevant next step made a broad finance pitch feel addressed to one buyer.
- [Brian’s Office](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/campaign/brians-office/): Ramp went looking for the world’s most famous accountant and found him at Dunder Mifflin. Brian Baumgartner, who played Kevin Malone on The Office, would sit in a glass box in Flatiron Plaza and do expense reports by hand. His opponent was Ramp, which said it automated 600,000 receipts a day. Casting Kevin made the setup instantly legible. Watching the pile grow made the product pitch just as easy to understand.
- [Expert Reddit AMAs](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/campaign/reddit-amas/): An AMA lets the audience choose the follow-up. Ramp put its product and economics experts in a format where their answers, rather than a prepared keynote, had to carry the session. The questions also gave the team a ready-made agenda for follow-up content.
- [Finance creator and expert education program](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/campaign/creator-education/): A useful Excel lesson can earn an hour that a product pitch never would. Ramp brought in finance practitioners to teach work its audience already needed to do. The expertise gave people a reason to register; a recurring program gave them a reason to return.
- [OnRamp: the event and its afterlife](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/campaign/onramp-2025/): A customer conference gives a product roadmap people, arguments and a room to land in. OnRamp put practitioners beside Ramp’s leaders, then turned the sessions into material people could use after the event.
- [Love Finance](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/campaign/love-finance/): Finance workers do not need a brand to tell them their profession is miserable. “Love Finance” gave them permission to enjoy the job and made the administrative friction the enemy. That choice gave separate product stories a shared emotional point of view.
- [Ramp AI Index / Economics Lab](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/campaign/ai-index/): Ramp had something most marketing teams cannot manufacture: a live view of what businesses spend. The AI Index turned that data into news people could cite. Each update gave journalists and researchers a fresh reason to return, even if they had no intention of buying Ramp.
- [Expenses Should Do Themselves](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/campaign/saquon-super-bowl/): Put a pile of receipts in front of Saquon Barkley and the waste of time is immediately obvious. Every second he spends sorting paper is a second you’d rather see him spend on the field. That’s the expense automation pitch in one image.
- [Treasury has landed](https://www.sushilathreya.com/ramp/campaign/treasury-wrecking-ball/): High returns or easy access to your cash? Ramp made the word “or” the villain. Smashing it into an ampersand made an abstract treasury pitch readable from across the street.
